summary: Offshore light 14.5 miles east of Cape Henry marking Chesapeake Bay: lightship LV-116 from 1933, steel Texas tower lit 1965, deactivated and sold in 2016.

structures.note: Prefabricated modules; steel pilings set 180 ft into the seabed and filled with concrete; 75 ft main structure with the light a further 42 ft above (117 ft to the centre of the lantern, USLHS and Light List).

facts.agency: Privately owned since the 2016 sale (LighthouseFriends); the buyer is not named in the sources read

access.note: Tower closed. Offshore, 14.5 miles east of Cape Henry; primarily reached by helicopter, with boat hoists and boarding ladders. Not open to visitors.

events.note: Lightship No. 116 (LV-116) built at Charleston, SC; placed first at Fenwick Island Shoal, Del.
Lightship moved to the Chesapeake Light station, 14.5 miles east of Virginia Beach (the lightship, not the station record's 1930 date)
September 1936 hurricane (17-19 Sept): ship parted moorings, spare mooring used, rode out under power, relieved, taken into port, repaired
Lighthouse Service vessels transferred to Coast Guard duty; LV-116 designated WLV-538
Armed with two 20 mm guns, painted gray; examination and guard vessel off the north end of the Cape Cod Canal
A very large wave damaged the lightship's pilothouse (LighthouseFriends)
Chesapeake Light tower commissioned 25 Sept 1965; lightship sailed to Delaware Bay
Three-phase automation campaign; all personnel then removed
COVE instruments mounted on the tower for NASA's CERES validation
Coast Guard considered demolition; testing found the tower structurally sound; it stayed an active aid
Transferred from the Coast Guard to the Department of Energy (October 2012)
GSA online auction ended 3 Aug 2016, high bid $215,000 (LighthouseFriends gives the amount; the buyer is not named in the sources read)
Ceased as an aid to navigation; instruments removed by December 2016

corrections.why: Light List Volume II (2011 copy) gives the height as 117 feet; LighthouseFriends gives 75 ft main structure plus 42 ft to the light (117 ft). 117 ft = 35.7 m.

Light List Volume II, introduction: column (6) is the nominal range in nautical miles, and the Chesapeake Light entry gives 19. LighthouseFriends says the range was sixteen miles (the story gives both). Wikipedia gives 19 miles (lead only).
Light List Volume II entry for the tower: Fl (2)W 15s. The current record's Fl W 4s is not found for this light in that edition.

The USLHS place record gives 'Year Established: 1930' (the lightship built and first placed that year at Fenwick Island Shoal, Del.). The lightship came to this station in 1933 and the tower was first lit in 1965 (LighthouseFriends; Chesapeake Chapter timeline). The record's 1930 matches the archive's 'established' year, so a human should decide whether first_lit means the station or the tower.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The sources differ on the start date. The USLHS place record gives 1930 as the year established. The lightship was built and first placed at Fenwick Island Shoal, Del., in 1930 (Bulletin 1930), and it came to this station in 1933 (LighthouseFriends; Chesapeake Chapter). The tower was first lit in 1965. The story uses 1933 for the lightship station and 1965 for the tower.
Record says inactive, deactivated 2016. LighthouseFriends: ceased as an aid to navigation in 2016 after the tower was sold at GSA auction. Consistent.

notes_for_editor: 1) The USLHS place record for 'Chesapeake' has coordinates 35.905, -75.713 (one degree south of the tower at 36.905, -75.713). The roster matched by name only (tool warning: 111 km from the station). The roster years (1966-1979) and the tower-era roles fit this light, so the match is accepted, but please check the place page. The place record also prints 'Height of light above mean high water, in feet: 400', which conflicts with the 117 ft in the same record and the Light List; not used. 2) The archive role 'Principal Lighthouse Keeper' is normalised to head keeper per STORY_GUIDE; the roster tool printed it as 'keeper'. 3) Alexander Andersen (first master of LV-116) is not on the USLHS roster for this place. A Bulletin 1937 separations notice (PDF p.44, OCR 'Alexander Andersen, master, Chesa. peake Lightship No. 116, retired') names a master of that name for this ship. It is not linked to the first master in the story because the link rests on the name and the ship; a human may decide. 4) Range: the Light List (Volume II introduction, column 6) gives nominal range in nautical miles and the entry gives 19. LighthouseFriends gives sixteen miles; both are in the story. Wikipedia gives 19 miles (lead only, not cited). 5) The 1935 master's report (Bulletin PDF p. 1) is checked against the OCR; the quoted sentence is clean. 6) The 1936 hurricane account (Bulletin PDF p. 35) has broken words in places; the story quotes only the clean phrases. The relief and return dates (19 and 25 September) are not quoted for that reason, though the OCR reads them as 19 and 25. The year 1936 for the storm comes from the 1936 Bulletin volume, not from the passage itself. 7) Garrison (Bulletin 1937 PDF p.48) and Tillette (PDF p.24) were checked on the page images: both are under 'Transfers and promotions' (printed pp.92 and 68). 8) LighthouseFriends' 1962 damage and the 1939 pay cut are LighthouseFriends' statements; no Bulletin text was found for them. 9) The Bulletin 1933 'Chesapeake' hit concerns a whistle buoy, not this station. 10) Wikipedia's Chesapeake Light article was used as a lead only. Its 'first established in 1930' is the record's date and is not cited. 11) LighthouseFriends gives the GSA auction as opening on 3 June 2016 and ending on 3 August 2016, with fifteen bidders; the buyer is not named in the sources read. 12) The story's '1933 to 1965' lightship span is from the Chesapeake Chapter and LighthouseFriends; the 1930 record date is disclosed in the story as a disagreement.
